title: Out of the Solar System
description: Walk from the surface of the Sun to Pluto. Eleven stops, scaled to whatever distance you choose — and a first-hand lesson in how much of the solar system is empty space.

media.caption: The Sun and the orbits of the planets, seen at an angle.
The Sun's churning surface, marked by darker sunspots.
Venus wrapped in featureless pale cloud.
Earth as a blue crescent, with weather systems over the ocean.
The rust-red disc of Mars, with a bright polar cap.
The dwarf planet Ceres, the largest body in the asteroid belt.
Jupiter's banded clouds and the Great Red Spot.
Saturn and its rings, casting a shadow across the planet.
Uranus as a near-featureless pale blue-green disc.
Deep blue Neptune, with faint white cloud streaks.
Pluto's pale heart-shaped plain of frozen nitrogen.

milestones.title: The Sun
milestones.body: You begin at the surface of the Sun, which holds about 99.8% of all the mass in the solar system. Its visible surface burns at roughly 5,500 °C, and the light leaving it now will take 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth. Everything ahead of you orbits this one object.

notification.title: Leaving the Sun
notification.body: Your journey starts at the surface of the Sun. Pluto is 5,906 million km ahead.

milestones.title: Mercury
milestones.body: The smallest planet and the closest to the Sun, orbiting it once every 88 days. With almost no atmosphere to hold heat, its day side reaches about 430 °C while its night side falls to around −180 °C. Its cratered surface has changed little in billions of years.

notification.title: Mercury
notification.body: 57.9 million km from the Sun. The smallest planet, and the fastest.

milestones.title: Venus
milestones.body: Nearly Earth's twin in size, and nothing like it otherwise. A dense carbon dioxide atmosphere presses down at about ninety times Earth's surface pressure and traps enough heat to hold the surface near 465 °C — hotter than Mercury, despite being further out.

notification.title: Venus
notification.body: 108.2 million km from the Sun. The hottest surface of any planet.

milestones.title: Earth
milestones.body: Home, and the only place known to carry life. Liquid water covers about 71% of the surface, and a magnetic field deflects the solar wind that stripped Mars bare. This distance from the Sun — 149.6 million km — is the yardstick astronomers call one astronomical unit.

notification.title: Earth
notification.body: 149.6 million km from the Sun. You are walking past home.

milestones.title: Mars
milestones.body: A cold desert with a thin carbon dioxide atmosphere, two small moons, and the largest volcano in the solar system: Olympus Mons, some 22 km high. Dry river channels and clay minerals show that water once ran across this surface.

notification.title: Mars
notification.body: 227.9 million km from the Sun. The last of the rocky planets.

milestones.title: The Asteroid Belt
milestones.body: A broad, mostly empty band of rock and metal between Mars and Jupiter. Its largest body, the dwarf planet Ceres, is about 940 km across; everything in the belt together adds up to only a few percent of the Moon's mass. Spacecraft pass straight through it without needing to dodge anything.

notification.title: The Asteroid Belt
notification.body: 413.7 million km from the Sun. Emptier than it looks in films.

milestones.title: Jupiter
milestones.body: More massive than every other planet combined, with more than ninety known moons. The Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth that has been turning for at least a century and a half. Jupiter has no solid surface — the banded clouds simply give way to hydrogen compressed until it behaves like a metal.

notification.title: Jupiter
notification.body: 778.5 million km from the Sun. You are now in the outer solar system.

milestones.title: Saturn
milestones.body: The rings are almost entirely water ice, in pieces ranging from dust grains to boulders the size of a house, spread across a span wider than the Earth–Moon distance but often only tens of metres thick. Saturn itself is less dense than water.

notification.title: Saturn
notification.body: 1,432 million km from the Sun. Sunlight here is about 1% as bright as on Earth.

milestones.title: Uranus
milestones.body: An ice giant tipped on its side, rotating at an axial tilt of about 98 degrees, so its poles take turns facing the Sun through a 42-year summer and a 42-year winter. Methane in the upper atmosphere absorbs red light and leaves the planet a flat blue-green.

notification.title: Uranus
notification.body: 2,867 million km from the Sun. Half your walk is behind you.

milestones.title: Neptune
milestones.body: Found in 1846 by working backwards from irregularities in Uranus's orbit — predicted on paper before anyone saw it. The fastest winds in the solar system tear through its atmosphere at up to 2,000 km/h, driven by an internal heat source rather than by sunlight, which arrives here about 900 times fainter than on Earth.

notification.title: Neptune
notification.body: 4,515 million km from the Sun. The last planet.

milestones.title: Pluto
milestones.body: Reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006, and still largely unknown until New Horizons flew past in July 2015 and found mountains of water ice and a vast, smooth glacier of frozen nitrogen. One Pluto year lasts 248 Earth years. Look back: the Sun is now just the brightest star in the sky.

notification.title: Pluto
notification.body: 5,906 million km from the Sun. You have crossed the solar system.
